title: rewrite node eviction API and plumb graceful lease termination
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: the current node eviction and lease handling in the GPU fleet controller is brittle. In high-churn scenarios (spot reclamations, rolling upgrades) nodes are force-evicted without a coordinated drain handshake with the serving runtime. This causes large KV-cache losses, long warmup tails, and sudden request failures that spike p99 latency and increase retry churn. The autoscaler reacts to these transient failures by over-provisioning, increasing cost and making tail latency worse.

Proposal: implement a dedicated LeaseTermination/Drainflow API and state machine that replaces the ad-hoc eviction signals. Key changes: (1) introduce ordered termination states (DrainRequested -> Draining -> ReadyToTerminate -> Terminated) persisted in the controller's backing store so restarts are idempotent; (2) plumb a short-lived grpc/gateway handshake between the controller and the serving runtime (drain endpoint) so the runtime can gracefully flush KV prefixes, snapshot hot caches, and refuse new long-lived requests; (3) change capacity planner to reserve the draining node's allocated slots until DrainConfirmed or drain-timeout; (4) throttle concurrent drains to avoid thundering-eviction storms and add per-node jitter; (5) upgrade controller dependencies (client-go and controller-runtime) to reduce reliance on deprecated APIs that made reconciler edge-cases hard to reason about.

Why now: recent incident INC-2025-003 highlighted cluster-wide p99 spikes during a spot reclaim wave; post-incident runbook and metrics analysis showed >40% of evictions were handled without an application-level drain, leading to a 3x increase in cold-cache tail latency. This refactor directly targets those failures and is expected to reduce average recovery token cost and improve overall SLOs.

Trade-offs: the new state machine adds complexity to the controller and requires small runtime changes (a lightweight drain endpoint). There is a small risk of extended capacity consumption during drain windows; mitigations below limit concurrent drains and provide timeouts. The plan favors availability and graceful degradation over immediate resource reclamation.
updates: 2025-01-15: Spike completed. PoC for DrainRequested/Draining states and a minimal gRPC drain handshake implemented against the local serving runtime mock. Found race between reconciler retry backoff and external drain confirmation; added idempotent tokens to avoid double-drain.

2025-01-22: Dependency upgrade plan drafted. Will bump k8s client-go to v0.27 and controller-runtime to v0.13 to use the newer cache invalidation hooks. Ran quick compile checks and fixed API shape changes in the controller scaffolding.

2025-01-30: Prototype benchmark: simulated 100 spot reclaims across 200-node staging. Baseline median recovery time 45s -> prototype 18s; p99 tail reduced by ~35%. Benchmark script and results uploaded to Confluence (link below).

2025-02-05: Architecture review with SRE and serving runtime leads (Sara Patel, Diego Ruiz). Feedback: add explicit metrics for lease_handshake_latency and drain_outcomes; require follow-up integration tests for state persistence across controller restarts. Action items added.

2025-02-12: Implemented controller-side throttling with a concurrency limit flag (default 5) and per-node jitter. Integration tests updated. Initial PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/1452

2025-02-20: Canary rollout plan approved. Feature-flagged rollout: canary 5% (internal infra), monitor 72h, ramp 25% -> 100% if no regression. Dashboard and alerts defined (latency, drain_failed_count, lease_handshake_failures).
acceptance_criteria: New LeaseTermination state persisted and reconciler resumes correctly after controller restart (unit + integration test coverage)
Serving runtime exposes drain endpoint and handshake completes in <=15s for 95% of drains in staging
Datadog dashboard shows drain_latency and drain_outcomes; no increase in eviction-related 5xxs during canary
Canary rollout executed and staged to 25% with no customer-facing regressions; full rollout or rollback decision documented
PRs merged and dependency upgrades landed (client-go v0.27, controller-runtime v0.13) without breaking other controllers
test_plan: Local: run controller + runtime mock harness with scripted evictions to validate state transitions
Staging: 200-node cluster, simulate spot reclaim wave (100-150 evictions), measure median and p99 recoveries
Chaos: inject controller restart during active drains to ensure idempotency and persistence
Canary: enable feature flag on 5% fleet and run production traffic for 72h with focused SLO alerts
Post-rollout: 2-week monitoring window to ensure sustained improvement and no regression in cost metrics
notes: Implementation detail: use per-node tombstone record with a generation UUID to avoid stale reconcile races when node objects are re-created by cloud provider
Backoff strategy: exponential backoff with capped jitter on reconcilers to avoid reconcilers thundering during large scale events
Observability: add tagging by cause (spot_reclaim, upgrade, admin_draining) so we can correlate failure modes to upstream causes
Rollout safety: config flag for max_concurrent_drains (cluster-level) and per-node max_drain_time; default conservative values chosen to balance reclamation speed and SLO stability
